routes.description: Establish that objective moral values require a transcendent standard of goodness and that objective duties require authoritative imperatives, then show that a necessarily good divine nature and commands grounded in that nature provide those foundations while naturalism does not.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects objective value to God's necessarily good nature, objective duty to competent divine authority, and the inadequacy of evolutionary, cultural, preference-based, or well-being facts to supply equivalent objective and binding foundations.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties have a supernatural rather than wholly natural ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Explain how God's necessarily good nature constitutes a nonarbitrary standard of objective moral value.
Explain how commands issued by competent divine authority and constrained by divine goodness constitute objective moral duties.
Show why natural facts about evolution, consciousness, preference, suffering, or flourishing do not alone establish objective moral value or binding obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the existence and ground of moral facts from moral language, moral knowledge, and disagreement about their application.
Account for the agency and responsibility presupposed by objective duties and address whether naturalistic determinism can sustain them.

routes.description: Establish that value arises through conscious experience, that facts about suffering and flourishing permit objective comparison and correction, and that rational scientific inquiry can investigate those facts, while showing that divine nature, commands, or revelation are unnecessary or unsuitable foundations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it derives an objective natural standard from conscious well-being, explains how inquiry can distinguish better and worse states independently of current opinion, and shows that supernatural authority neither supplies a necessary standard nor resolves arbitrariness and harmful-command objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral values and duties can be founded in natural facts about conscious creatures without supernatural authority.

centralBridges.description: Establish conscious experience as the domain in which suffering, flourishing, and morally relevant value can exist.
Explain how movement away from extreme misery toward flourishing supports objective comparisons and allows preferences, practices, and judgments to be mistaken.
Show how objective reasoning and scientific inquiry can investigate natural facts governing conscious well-being despite foundational axioms and first-person experience.
Show why defining divine nature as good or grounding duties in commands does not independently establish goodness and can conflict with judgments about suffering and harm.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend well-being as a usable objective standard despite incomplete definitions, plural forms of flourishing, and difficult boundary cases.
Address whether competing revelations, inherited traditions, and disputed purported commands provide reliable access to moral truth.

sections.title: The Ontological Ground of Objective Moral Value
sections.rationale: This issue tests the primary competing foundations: necessarily good divine nature on the supernatural route and conscious experience, suffering, and flourishing on the natural route.

sections.title: Well-Being, Moral Objectivity, and Scientific Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether natural facts permit objective comparisons, correction of preferences and cultures, and rational investigation despite axioms, subjective experience, or imprecise boundaries.

sections.title: From Facts to Objective Duties and Responsibility
sections.rationale: This issue addresses how either route moves from descriptions or values to binding obligations, including authority, the fact-value distinction, agency, ability, and responsibility.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Command, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether divine nature constrains commands nonarbitrarily and whether commands involving apparent harm can be assessed by a standard independent of their asserted source.

sections.title: Moral Ontology, Knowledge, Disagreement, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue distinguishes moral reality from access to it and tests the significance of disagreement, competing religious traditions, inherited belief, and shared inquiry for each foundational route.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties are independent of human opinion and require a sound foundation that theism supplies but atheism does not.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Craig, and the uninterrupted opening address begins immediately after the timing cue.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive thesis, so no earlier opposing move supplies response components for it to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the two conditionals and their direct relationship to the motion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two conditional claims are recoverable, and Craig expressly limits the speech by declining to argue that God exists.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional framing is explicit, but the necessity of the foundation is announced before the required grounding argument is supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure is consistent and intelligible, though this thesis alone does not establish either conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies a clear argumentative program but no independent support at this stage for the exclusive foundation claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly frames the supernatural-foundation motion and states the exact route-completion claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move announces Craig's own conditional case and does not materially interpret a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig states that theism supplies a sound objective foundation and atheism does not, expressly identifying both assertions as conditional.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's necessarily holy and loving nature grounds objective moral values, while divine commands consistent with that nature constitute objective moral duties.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Craig's explicitly announced opening speech and develops his labeled first contention in a continuous first-person presentation.

response.rationale: This is a constructive account with no earlier opposing locked move available as a response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the proposed grounds for both objective values and objective duties.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nature-versus-command division is explicit, and commands are expressly qualified as consistent with holiness and love.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is stated categorically, while the excerpt asserts rather than fully defends why divine nature constitutes objective value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between values grounded in nature and duties constituted by commands is coherent, with one compressed grounding bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage specifies the theory but offers little independent warrant for necessary divine goodness or command-generated obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable divine-nature bridge and also materially advances the divine-command bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage presents Craig's positive account without developing or characterizing a live competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig grounds values in God's nature and duties in commands, adding that commands must accord with a holy and loving nature.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: On atheistic naturalism, evolved human moral beliefs and concern for human welfare are adaptive products without an objective basis that privileges them over other biological dispositions.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly turns to his second contention, and the same uninterrupted opening speech continues through the naturalistic and evolutionary argument.

response.rationale: This opening constructive criticism has no earlier opposing locked move eligible for formal response targeting.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances naturalism's alleged grounding deficit but compresses the central inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic challenge is recoverable, but movement between atheism, naturalism, evolutionary origin, and objective worth is only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical grounding deficit exceeds the support supplied by evolutionary origin and cosmic transience without excluding rival naturalist accounts.

charity.alternative: Naturalism may treat evolved cognition as access to stance-independent welfare facts rather than as their ontological creator.
charity.decisiveQualification: An evolutionary genealogy of belief does not by itself show that every natural candidate for objective value is illusory.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from accidental evolutionary origin and finitude to absence of objective worth leaves a substantial unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolution and transience are invoked generally, without evidence or comparison showing that all natural objective-value theories fail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The argument directly supports the central claim that naturalistic evolutionary facts cannot ground objective moral value.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presses an important genealogy challenge but substantially underrepresents naturalist realist alternatives to adaptive preference.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig describes humans as evolved accidental byproducts and asks what objective basis could privilege their worth or moral dispositions.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Defining moral goodness as conscious-creature well-being makes the claim that maximizing well-being is good tautological and does not explain why well-being is objectively morally valuable.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig names Harris and his proposed solution directly while continuing the same clearly attributed opening address without a speaker transition.

response.rationale: Although described as a criticism of Harris, chronology makes it an opening constructive move with no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it isolates a direct definitional objection to the natural well-being route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The circularity objection is clear, though it implicitly assumes Harris offers an identity definition rather than a substantive reduction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the maneuver a mere trick overstates what follows unless the competing reductive interpretation is first excluded.

charity.alternative: Harris may be proposing a substantive naturalistic identity or domain thesis rather than a merely verbal redefinition of good.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even on that reading, he still owes a bridge from conscious well-being to specifically moral goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection validly exposes circularity under a stipulated-definition reading, but its application depends on a disputed interpretation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited formulation supports the concern, though the excerpt does not establish that Harris intends only a tautological definition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central objective-well-being bridge by challenging the proposed identification of well-being with moral goodness.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig identifies the surviving bridge problem but frames the opposing position too narrowly as simple verbal stipulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig quotes the proposal to define good by conscious-creature well-being and argues that the resulting maximization claim becomes tautological.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Natural science describes facts but cannot generate objective obligations, which require authoritative moral imperatives rather than evolutionary advantage, taboo, or social conditioning.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig introduces a distinct second question about duties and sustains the argument in the same uninterrupted opening speech.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive account, and no earlier opposing locked move exists for response-component analysis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely addresses the source of obligation and distinguishes facts from authoritative imperatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fact-norm and authority claims are clear, but science, naturalism, animals, and obligation are treated with broad implicit scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move categorically excludes natural obligation without defending why authoritative imperatives are necessary or uniquely divine.

charity.alternative: A naturalist may ground duties in objective reasons arising from welfare, agency, or relations rather than in commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: Descriptive science alone does not yield obligations unless some normative bridge or reason-conferring principle is defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The fact-norm distinction is coherent, but the conclusion that obligation requires commanding authority is a substantial unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies mainly on assertion about science, animals, and authority without comparing plausible natural accounts of obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable divine-command account of duties while attacking the competing natural-duty route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The fact-norm gap is fairly identified, but the move largely omits non-command naturalist theories of normative reasons.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says science reports how matters are, not what ought to be, and proposes authoritative commands as the missing basis of obligation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If human actions are causally determined without relevant freedom or control, the responsibility presupposed by objective moral duty is unavailable.
moves.attributionBasis: The same speaker labels this as a second problem and explicitly attributes the determinist position and its implications to Harris.

response.rationale: Despite addressing Harris's published position, this opening move has no earlier opposing locked move eligible as a formal target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a clear responsibility challenge but does not defend its incompatibilist premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional is recoverable, but free will shifts from relevant control to an unqualified category without explaining alternatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that no free will entails no responsibility is categorical despite the absence of a defended responsibility criterion.

charity.alternative: Responsibility may be compatibilist, reasons-responsive, or revisionary even if libertarian freedom is absent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cited Harris position reportedly rejects compatibilism, but that does not independently establish Craig's general incompatibilist inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if the unargued premise that responsibility requires the disputed kind of freedom is accepted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt attributes determinism and a social-construct view to Harris, but gives limited support for the universal philosophical conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary agency-and-responsibility bridge rather than the motion or a central grounding bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notes Harris's unusually broad denial but does not engage the strongest nonlibertarian accounts of responsible control.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig attributes causal determinism and rejection of libertarian and compatibilist freedom to Harris, then denies resulting objective responsibility.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Conscious experience is a necessary condition for value because changes in the universe can matter only if they can affect a conscious system.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly announces his reduction of value to conscious-creature well-being and then develops the consciousness component in his own continuous speech.

response.rationale: This is Harris's constructive case and therefore has no response-component target among earlier opposing locked moves.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, the rock-universe contrast clearly and directly supports consciousness as a necessary condition of value.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly limited to a necessary condition: changes must at least potentially matter to a conscious system.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessary-condition force fits the thought experiment and does not itself assert that consciousness is sufficient for morality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contrast coherently supports the narrower claim that value requires possible significance for conscious experience.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment strongly supports the intuition, though it does not compare nonexperiential theories of value in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly establishes the central consciousness-value bridge on the natural route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops Harris's positive necessary-condition claim without interpreting a substantive opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts a universe containing only rocks with one containing conscious systems and limits mattering to effects on consciousness.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: The worst possible misery for every conscious creature is bad, supplying a minimal objective standard from which better states and factual mistakes about moral progress follow.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly turns from consciousness to well-being and carries the worst-misery thought experiment through the final delivered row of this argumentative move.

response.rationale: This constructive move has no earlier opposing locked target requiring response-component classification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a vivid minimal standard and connects it directly to objective better-or-worse comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable as a minimal starting point concerning universal maximal misery, not a complete moral theory.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The badness of universal maximal misery is strongly supported, but broader claims about moral progress require additional comparative principles.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The minimal bad-state premise supports some objective comparisons, though the bridge to a general moral landscape remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The extreme case is powerful and representative for a minimal standard, but does not document how all difficult comparisons are resolved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge from misery and flourishing to objective welfare comparisons.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a positive thought experiment without materially construing an opponent's alternative position.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris asks the audience to imagine maximum suffering for every conscious creature and treats its badness as the minimal assumption.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Because moral questions concern conscious experience, minds are natural phenomena, and natural facts govern well-being, moral truth can be investigated scientifically.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation occurs within Harris's speech and develops his characteristic moral-landscape account.

response.rationale: This is a constructive scientific-inquiry argument, so it has no earlier opposing response components to classify.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it explicitly connects minds, natural law, welfare facts, and scientific investigation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The core chain is clear, but science ranges from empirical investigation to rational understanding, and moral truth is broadly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Natural dependence supports scientific relevance, but does not alone establish that science can settle every normative component.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from minds being natural to morality being scientifically understandable leaves one material normative and methodological bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The natural-dependence premises are plausible, but representative scientific findings and a defended norm-to-value warrant are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central rational-inquiry bridge governing investigation of natural facts about conscious well-being.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage states Harris's positive naturalistic inference without substantially interpreting an opponent's alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris argues that moral questions depend on experience, minds are natural, and natural facts influence conscious-creature well-being.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Conduct and preferences can be objectively mistaken when they reliably frustrate creaturely well-being, independently of whether individuals or cultures presently endorse them.
moves.attributionBasis: The continuous remarks remain in Harris's speech, with explicit first-person examples and a direct reference to Craig's contrary position.

components.text: Naturalism allegedly lacks an objective basis for ranking evolved human values over competing biological dispositions.
Natural facts allegedly cannot make conduct or preferences objectively wrong without an authoritative imperative.

response.rationale: Harris directly denies that all value judgments are merely relative to other preferences and argues that values can be defective by reliably frustrating well-being; this contacts both grounding and duty criticisms, though it does not fully explain binding obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer reaches the decisive objective-standard component but leaves the separate authority-to-obligation demand underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objective mistake is tied to frustrated well-being, though the types of conduct, preference, and cultural judgment covered remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support some objectively defective preferences, but the categorical conclusion needs a fuller defense of well-being's authority.

charity.alternative: Craig's objection may allow objective welfare facts while denying that they are identical to moral value or binding duty.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that preferences frustrate welfare answers relativism only if welfare is independently established as morally authoritative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The error criterion works given well-being as the standard, but the moral authority of that standard remains a material implicit premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete harmful practices illustrate frustrated welfare, though the general criterion and its independence from evaluative premises remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central naturalism-grounding-deficit bridge by proposing an objective natural error standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris rebuts simple preference relativism but does not fully confront the stronger ontological and authority-based version of Craig's demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris rejects parity among all preferences and uses practices affecting girls' well-being to illustrate objectively mistaken values.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Science itself depends on values such as evidence, logical consistency, understanding, and intellectual honesty, so a categorical fact-value divide cannot exclude morality from rational inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted conclusion of Harris's speech presents a first-person scientific example before the applause and moderator transition.

response.rationale: This constructive analogy has no formal reply target despite bearing on Craig's earlier fact-norm criticism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it materially supports rational inquiry, although epistemic values do not alone establish moral values.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy is clear, but value encompasses epistemic norms and moral value without fully distinguishing their normative roles.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Science plausibly presupposes epistemic standards, but that point is insufficient by itself to dissolve the moral fact-value distinction.

charity.alternative: A defender of the fact-value distinction can accept epistemic norms while denying that empirical facts entail moral obligations.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy shows that inquiry is value-laden, not that epistemic and moral normativity share the same ground or content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The premises support rejection of wholly value-free inquiry, but the extension to moral inquiry contains a material analogy gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The chemistry example concretely illustrates epistemic standards, while the claimed consequence for morality remains only indirectly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports rational inquiry into well-being, though it is less direct than an account of moral measurement or inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly exposes value commitments in science but does not address the strongest distinction between epistemic and moral norms.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris uses disagreement about water's composition to show science relies on evidence, consistency, understanding, and intellectual standards.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The meaning and use of moral language must be distinguished from moral ontology: values are grounded in God's character and duties in divine commands, not in definitions of moral words.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig immediately before this first-person rebuttal, which explicitly restates his two contentions and addresses Harris by name.

components.text: Natural minds and welfare-governing facts allegedly make moral truth amenable to scientific investigation.
Values may be objectively mistaken when they reliably frustrate well-being.

response.rationale: Craig usefully distinguishes word meaning from ontological grounding and restates his own account, but he does not answer the inference from natural minds to scientific inquiry or Harris's welfare-based error criterion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is relevant contrary material but not an answer to the decisive natural-inquiry or objective-error components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The semantic-versus-ontological distinction and the separate grounds of values and duties are clearly and stably stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction is sound, but dismissing the opposing material as irrelevant exceeds what the excerpt's restatement establishes.

charity.alternative: Harris's well-being thesis can be an ontological naturalist proposal rather than merely a definition of moral vocabulary.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even as ontology, the proposal still requires a defended identity or grounding relation between welfare and moral goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The semantics-ontology distinction is coherent, though restating divine grounds does not independently resolve the competing ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is supported by exposition, but divine grounding is asserted and the rival naturalist reading is not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary ontology-epistemology bridge rather than completing a central or motion-level bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig preserves the legitimate grounding demand but too readily treats Harris's positive naturalist account as merely semantic.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig distinguishes definitions from ontology, then restates that God's character grounds values and commands ground duties.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because good and evil persons could share well-being in a possible world, well-being and moral goodness are not identical and natural facts about flourishing alone cannot ground moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig attributes the relevant admissions to Harris's book and develops the modal identity argument continuously in his rebuttal.

components.text: The welfare continuum allegedly supplies an objective moral standard connecting better states with moral goodness.
Natural facts governing welfare allegedly suffice for scientific understanding of moral truth.

response.rationale: Craig explicitly argues that a possible divergence between well-being and moral goodness defeats their identity and states the consequence that welfare facts alone cannot ground moral value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly targets the identity inference and gives the modal counterexample's defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument clearly concerns identity rather than mere correlation and explicitly invokes a possible divergence as its test.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A genuine possible divergence defeats strict identity, though it would not defeat every grounding, dependence, or constitutive account.

charity.alternative: Well-being may ground or constitute moral goodness without being strictly identical to every point on a welfare continuum.
charity.decisiveQualification: The modal argument directly defeats identity only if Harris's case requires that strong identity rather than a looser grounding relation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modal nonidentity inference is strong against strict identity, with one bounded gap in extending it to all natural grounding.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument invokes an attributed possible-world concession, but the exact rival thesis and full scenario are only partially documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central objective-well-being bridge by challenging the identity needed to convert welfare into moral goodness.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig identifies a serious modal qualification but overstates the result as incoherence for every possible well-being account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig invokes a possible divergence between the well-being continuum and the moral landscape to reject their strict identity.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Defining God as intrinsically good does not independently ground goodness, while beginning moral science from the badness of universal maximal misery is an axiomatic move comparable to those used in other sciences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Harris, and the ensuing uninterrupted first-person response directly addresses Craig by name.

components.text: God's necessarily good nature allegedly supplies a nonarbitrary ontological standard of moral value.
A well-being axiom allegedly constitutes an illicit definitional maneuver rather than a substantive moral foundation.

response.rationale: Harris directly applies Craig's definitional criticism to intrinsic divine goodness and contrasts that move with the explicit axiom of universal maximal misery, contacting both demands without fully proving the asymmetry.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts both decisive components but only partially explains why the welfare axiom is epistemically superior.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison between intrinsic divine goodness and an axiomatic misery premise is clear and appropriately limited to grounding.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Harris qualifies the evil-god point as what he can see and presents the definitional symmetry as a challenge rather than a proof.

charity.alternative: Craig may offer essential goodness as a metaphysical entailment of maximal greatness, not as an arbitrary verbal definition.
charity.decisiveQualification: That entailment still needs an account of why maximal greatness includes recognizable moral goodness rather than merely stipulating it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry challenge is coherent, though the claimed superiority of the misery axiom requires a further noncircular justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt accurately identifies the definitional form and offers an extreme experiential axiom, but provides limited comparative defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central divine-nature-values bridge and supports the supernatural-critique bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris exposes a genuine symmetry concern but does not yet address the strongest maximal-greatness explanation later supplied by Craig.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris argues that intrinsic divine goodness is itself a definitional move and compares it with his maximal-misery starting axiom.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God's essential goodness follows from the concept of a maximally great and worship-worthy being rather than from an arbitrary stipulative definition.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator begins the closing speeches, and Craig's first-person closing explicitly summarizes and defends his initial contention.

components.text: Defining God as intrinsically good allegedly fails to supply an independent, nonarbitrary ground of goodness.

response.rationale: Craig directly answers that goodness is entailed by maximal greatness and worship-worthiness rather than arbitrarily appended, but does not independently defend why those concepts entail moral goodness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive stipulation objection is explicitly contacted, with one important explanatory bridge left compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conceptual-entailment reply is recoverable, though maximal greatness and worship-worthiness carry an implicit moral qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig states conceptual entailment confidently, but the bachelor analogy does not itself establish the contested content of God.

charity.alternative: The critic can accept the stipulated concept while asking whether it explains goodness rather than builds goodness into the label.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conceptual entailment blocks arbitrariness only if maximal greatness and worship-worthiness independently and noncircularly include moral goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is coherent given the proposed concept of God, but the crucial inclusion of moral goodness remains underargued.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The bachelor analogy illustrates entailment but supplies limited warrant that maximal greatness necessarily contains the relevant moral properties.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-nature-values bridge against the definitional-arbitrariness objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig accurately answers the simple stipulation objection but only partly reaches the stronger explanatory-circularity challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig compares God's essential goodness to conceptual truths and grounds it in maximal greatness and worship-worthiness.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Because materially similar apologetic reasoning supports incompatible religions, accidental birthplace and inherited doctrine make sectarian revelation an unreliable basis for moral knowledge and eternal consequences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator assigns the closing to Harris, whose first-person argument contrasts Craig and Christianity with Islam.

components.text: God's essential goodness allegedly follows from maximal greatness and worship-worthiness rather than arbitrary definition.
Divine nature and commands allegedly provide an objective moral foundation.

response.rationale: The argument raises a serious epistemic symmetry among incompatible revelations but does not answer the conceptual entailment of essential goodness or the ontological divine-command account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material about access and reliability, not an answer to the selected ontological components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The revelation-symmetry challenge is clear, though the claim that the apologetic logic is exactly the same is broadly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Material similarity is plausible, but exact equivalence and unreliability require closer comparison of evidence and doctrines.

charity.alternative: Competing religions may share formal apologetic patterns while differing materially in historical evidence, doctrine, and moral content.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared form and birthplace dependence still create an access problem unless discriminating evidence is independently supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Competing incompatible claims support an underdetermination concern, but similarity alone does not prove equal credibility or falsity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Islam is a concrete comparison, though the claim of materially identical reasoning is asserted rather than demonstrated in representative detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary revelation-reliability bridge rather than a central ontological foundation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The symmetry objection retains force, but the claim of exact sameness omits potentially decisive evidential differences.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris argues that similar apologetic reasoning can defend Christianity and Islam and highlights birthplace-dependent inherited belief.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Moral and spiritual truth should be pursued through present honest inquiry into the conditions of human flourishing rather than through competing sectarian claims about an invisible God.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is the uninterrupted conclusion of Harris's closing and states his alternative to sectarian moral authority.

components.text: A maximally great, worship-worthy God's essential goodness allegedly grounds objective values.
Moral ontology should be separated from language, knowledge, and disputed access.

response.rationale: Harris proposes honest inquiry into flourishing as an epistemic alternative to sectarianism, but he does not answer the ontological claim about essential divine goodness or Craig's ontology-access distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move is issue-bearing and relevant to access, yet the decisive selected ontological components remain uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The preference for inquiry is clear, but honest inquiry, faith, evidence, and flourishing are broad and lack procedural boundaries.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling honest inquiry the only needed tool exceeds the support supplied and understates unresolved normative starting points.

charity.alternative: Sectarian traditions may incorporate evidence, reasoning, moral experience, and internal methods of correction rather than replacing inquiry wholesale.
charity.decisiveQualification: Competing unverifiable authority claims still require shared discriminating standards to justify public moral knowledge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed epistemic preference is intelligible, but the exclusive conclusion and link to objective foundations remain substantially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Religious fragmentation illustrates the concern, while the sufficiency of honest inquiry and absence of compelling evidence are mostly asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary revelation-reliability bridge through a proposed shared method of moral inquiry.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a real public-reason concern but portrays the contrast between faith and inquiry too categorically.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts competing invisible-God claims with present inquiry into the conditions under which human beings flourish.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Grounding morality solely in competent authority collapses the distinction between genuine harms and conventional rules, whereas moral understanding independently tracks effects on well-being.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly asks to add a point, identifies Craig's authority-based account, and develops his previously introduced psychopathy argument.

components.text: Objective obligation allegedly requires competent authoritative imperatives rather than natural facts about flourishing.
Divine commands consistent with a good nature allegedly constitute moral duties.

response.rationale: Harris directly challenges authority's sufficiency by contrasting permission-dependent classroom rules with independently recognized harms; he contacts both authority claims but does not fully address commands constrained by essential goodness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive authority component is contacted, while the divine-goodness constraint receives only a partial answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between conventional permission and harm-based moral violation is clear and illustrated with bounded examples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example supports the limited claim that competent authority alone does not erase the ordinary distinction between convention and harm.

charity.alternative: Craig's authority is divine and constrained by perfect goodness, not equivalent to a teacher's unconstrained classroom permission.
charity.decisiveQualification: The example refutes bare authority but not necessarily commands whose authority and content are independently fixed by essential goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example coherently distinguishes authority-created convention from harm, though its extension to constrained divine authority is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The classroom contrast is concrete and probative against bare authority, but no broader developmental or philosophical support is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central divine-commands-duties bridge by challenging authority as the constitutive source of moral obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris fairly tests authority alone but materially weakens the complete divine-command account by omitting its goodness constraint.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris contrasts teacher permission to drink soda with permission to punch someone, arguing that children recognize harm independently of authority.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: A deity that genuinely commanded sacrifice or comparable violence would thereby be evil, because the morality of the command can be judged independently of its purported divine source.
moves.attributionBasis: The statement is Harris's immediate first-person rejoinder to Craig's direct address and continues Harris's independent moral-evaluation argument.

components.text: Commands grounded in God's holy and loving nature allegedly constitute objective duties without arbitrariness.
A maximally great and worship-worthy God allegedly cannot issue an evil command.

response.rationale: Harris directly states that an actual sacrificial or violent command would make its issuer evil, asserting an independent moral test; the terse reply contacts both claims but does not defend that test.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive independent-judgment component is contacted, but the very brief answer leaves the divine-nature constraint substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Despite its brevity, the conditional claim is clear: if God issued the relevant command, that act would warrant judging God evil.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confidence fits the stated extreme case, though the moral criterion and disputed context are not defended in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: A necessarily good God could not genuinely issue an evil command, so an apparent command would instead be misidentified or misunderstood.
charity.decisiveQualification: That response risks insulating the theory unless apparent commands can be assessed by independently accessible moral criteria.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional independent-judgment claim is coherent, but it presupposes rather than argues for the standard used to classify the command.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt is only a terse assertion and supplies no developed evidence or warrant for resolving the disputed command scenario.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central supernatural critique by asserting that harmful commands remain independently morally assessable.

representationalCharity.rationale: The rejoinder identifies the epistemic circularity concern but does not engage the strongest impossibility claim in any detail.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris responds that if God genuinely issued the disputed violent command, that fact would make God evil.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Disagreement about applied morality concerns epistemic access rather than moral ontology, while objective values and duties require a transcendent ground beyond organisms, culture, and opinion.
moves.attributionBasis: The final audience question is expressly directed to Craig, and the answer restates his first-speech distinction and supernatural foundation argument.

components.text: Competing inherited revelations allegedly undermine the objective supernatural foundation because they produce incompatible moral claims.
Shared honest inquiry allegedly should replace sectarian revelation as the route to moral truth.

response.rationale: Craig expressly diagnoses disagreement as an epistemic-access issue rather than an ontological-grounding issue and states the defeating consequence that such disagreement does not answer his foundation claim; he also recognizes shared moral judgments but does not solve revelation reliability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly identifies the category distinction and its consequence, while leaving the independent access concern intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: Applied disagreement, epistemic perception, and ontological foundation are expressly distinguished, making the reply's scope readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction successfully blocks a direct ontological inference, but the renewed claim that atheism cannot ground value remains underwarranted.

charity.alternative: The revelation objection may target reliable access and public justification rather than purport to disprove moral ontology directly.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even so, epistemic disagreement does not by itself show that objective moral facts or a supernatural ground do not exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemology-ontology distinction is valid and directly applied, though the appended animal-machine conclusion repeats an unsupported grounding inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual diagnosis is well supported by the disagreement example, while the broader atheism and free-will claims remain asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary ontology-epistemology bridge, but does not itself complete the motion route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig accurately isolates the ontological non sequitur while leaving the strongest independent epistemic objection available.
